query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: W-based refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit superconducting properties at cryogenic temperatures due to tungsten’s potential to enhance electron–phonon interactions within a homogeneous alloy matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, homogeneous W-based refractory high-entropy alloy as formed under controlled casting conditions.
generation.intervention: Cooling the alloy to ultra-low (cryogenic) temperatures below an estimated critical temperature (e.g., <2 K) while minimizing external magnetic fields.
generation.conditions: Cryogenic environment with controlled impurities and minimal external magnetic perturbations; the alloy should retain a uniform microstructure during cooling.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform distribution of tungsten atoms within the alloy’s FCC (or similar) matrix is expected to mediate enhanced electron–phonon coupling necessary for superconductivity.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten’s inherent characteristics could foster stronger electron–phonon coupling even in a complex alloy system. This may allow the formation of Cooper pairs and the emergence of a superconducting phase when cooled below the critical temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: A transition to zero electrical resistance accompanied by evidence of the Meissner effect (magnetic flux expulsion) when the alloy is cooled below the critical temperature.
generation.baseline: Measurements taken at temperatures well above the predicted critical temperature, where the alloy exhibits normal metallic conduction and no superconducting behavior.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may not hold if phase separation or microstructural inhomogeneity occurs during alloy processing, if impurities disrupt tungsten’s electron–phonon coupling, or if the alloy matrix does not support coherent pairing over sufficient length scales.
generation.uncertainty: Due to limited prior studies linking tungsten-based high-entropy alloys to superconductivity, the exact critical temperature and the robustness of the superconducting phase remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of a W-based refractory high-entropy alloy with verified homogeneous microstructure. Cool samples incrementally in a cryostat while monitoring electrical resistance and magnetic susceptibility across the temperature range from above 10 K down to below 1 K.
measurements: Electrical resistance as a function of temperature
Magnetic susceptibility (to detect the Meissner effect)
Microstructural analysis (using TEM or XRD) pre- and post-cooling to ensure phase stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy does not display a transition to zero electrical resistance and fails to exhibit magnetic flux exclusion (Meissner effect) at temperatures below the expected critical temperature, then the hypothesis that the W-based high-entropy alloy exhibits superconductivity is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ].
